extracted.intended_audience: researchers and editors concerned with research integrity, scientific publishing, and post-publication review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and expectations for how journals, institutions, and the scientific community should detect, investigate, disclose, and act on suspected data manipulation or other serious problems in published papers. Focuses on image authenticity, availability of raw data, investigation independence and timeliness, and appropriate editorial responses (correction / expression of concern / retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of original/raw data for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Original microscopy (and other primary) data should be available to verify the accuracy of published figures and to resolve concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PNAS noted that "the original microscopy data is no longer available to further verify the accuracy of the images in question," highlighting that lack of raw data prevents verification. The post argues that inability to produce original images undermines the ability of editors/investigators to confirm whether image-processing errors or manipulation occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of images — absence of duplications/transversions/manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures and micrographs should be authentic and free of inappropriate duplications, transversions, or other manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors raised "massive data duplications and alterations" and provided multiple lines of evidence suggesting substantial amounts of data "may not be authentic." Examples include duplicated or replaced micrographs; the Retraction cited "data duplications and transversions." The page treats such irregularities as grounds for retraction or formal concern rather than minor correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent institutional investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspected misconduct should be investigated by an independent committee (institutional or external) and the complainants can request such an independent inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Letter-of-Concern explicitly "requested that an independent committee should investigate this matter." The timeline recounts UCSD convening an Investigation Committee and submitting reports to the Office of Research Integrity (ORI), showing the expected institutional investigative route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of investigation and editorial action
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and journals should act promptly: investigations, interviews, and editorial notices (corrections, expressions of concern, retractions) should not be excessively delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter contrasts Cell’s "quite rapid response" with PNAS’s "not-so-rapid response," documents ~16 months to initial committee interviews and further delays before reports reached ORI. Commenters criticize lengthy waits; the post calls for timely disclosure of investigation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate editorial response: correction vs expression of concern vs retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should choose an appropriate public response (correction, expression of concern, or retraction) consistent with the seriousness of problems and with ongoing investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors were "disturbed that PNAS should consider it acceptable to post such substantial data corrections... under ORI investigation." The post urged PNAS to publish an Expression of Concern or retract the paper. The PNAS editors later issued an expression of concern noting corrections and unavailable original data, illustrating editorial decision-making when evidence is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public availability of investigation findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The main findings of institutional or ORI investigations should be made available to the scientific community without undue delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors "call upon UCSD and ORI to make the main findings of their investigation available without further delay." The post emphasizes that more than three years after the start of a formal investigation the community still had not been informed of the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough documentation when raising concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints/letters raising concerns should include extensive documentation and clear evidence to support allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Letter-of-Concern was "extensively documented (54 pages)" and provided "multiple lines of evidence" regarding suspected inauthentic data. The page implies that detailed documentation strengthens the case and facilitates investigation and editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and peer-review rigor, avoiding membership fast-tracks
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must apply rigorous peer review and avoid expedited or less-rigorous pathways based solely on society membership or privileged communicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the PNAS paper was "communicated... within 10 days between submission and acceptance," and commenters criticize an "antiquated PNAS policy of letting members’ articles in so quickly and without any possibility of serious review." This is presented as a potential source of poor-quality or insufficiently vetted publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active post-publication peer review and community notification
rubrics_metrics.description: When problems are suspected, authors and concerned scientists should notify relevant peers and use post-publication review mechanisms to alert the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter was sent to "about 80 leading labs" and the post references PubPeer and community commentary. Commenters describe contacting thousands of scientists; the page endorses community-led scrutiny as essential to policing the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise characterization of reasons for retraction (fabrication vs error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices should clearly and accurately state whether problems arose from inadvertent errors or from data fabrication/fraud when appropriate evidence exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Retraction reportedly stated duplications and transversions but "did not refer to the mistakes as data fabrication." The post highlights the importance of clear language so readers understand the severity and nature of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of downstream impact (citations) when addressing problematic papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial and institutional actions should account for the paper’s influence (citations and use by others) when deciding corrective measures and communicating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the paper "has been cited 159 times," implying that widely cited problematic work has greater potential harm and urgency for correction or retraction and for notifying readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship responsibility and senior-author accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: All co-authors, especially senior and corresponding authors, should be accountable for the integrity of the data; journals/investigations should consider co-author roles and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary criticizes co-authors who "are happy to bask in the glory... with least concern about the authenticity of the data," and notes puzzling authorship/order shifts between the two papers. The page treats author accountability as an evaluative consideration in misconduct cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent journal policy on expressions of concern and follow-up actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should have consistent policies for issuing expressions of concern and for following up (e.g., awaiting institutional findings but ensuring timely public notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter observed PNAS "rarely publishes" expressions of concern and often states it is "awaiting the findings" of investigations. The post implies journals should apply EoCs consistently and ensure they are followed by appropriate next steps once investigations conclude.
